Main & Machine Sample / One workflow, one page

# An invoice follow-up plan.

Illustrative example. Not a client result.

Example situation: a small commercial maintenance business follows up on overdue invoices manually. Payment updates and customer replies live in different places, so each reminder needs another check.

## The recommendation Fix the status first.

Start with a reliable overdue-invoice list and your accounting system’s reminder features. AI may help draft unusual replies; it should not decide what a customer owes. The accounting ledger remains the source of truth.

Assign one person to check payments, credits, disputes, and promised payment dates before anything goes out.

## The proposed workflow Prepare. Review. Record.

- Prepare: pull open invoices from the accounting system into a review list. Use a saved message for routine reminders.

- Review: a named person checks the live balance and approves each send. Conflicting records or disputed invoices stay on hold.

- Record: save the reminder and any reply against the invoice. Pause follow-up when payment arrives or the customer raises an issue.

## Copy and adapt A reminder you can use.

Subject: Checking in on invoice [number]

Hi [name], our records show invoice [number] for [amount], due [date], is open. Could you confirm the payment status? If you’ve already paid or something needs correcting, please let me know.

Thank you,
[sender]

Replace the brackets and verify the details before sending.

## A small test Check whether it helps.

For one week, record time spent per reminder, records needing correction, and reminders sent in error. Compare with the current process before widening the test.

Success means: less checking time without more incorrect reminders. Stop if payment status cannot be verified reliably. No savings estimate is justified yet.

## Before a build Answer three questions.

Can your accounting system already support this flow? Who owns approval and exceptions? How will payments and replies update the list?

This proposal assumes usable invoice records, access to current payment status, and an accountable reviewer. Check those assumptions first.

## Budget context Standard features first.

This example is not a project quote. If custom work is justified, our paid audit is $3,500–$8,500 ; implementation sprints are $18,000–$60,000 . A fixed quote follows an agreed scope.

Ongoing care is optional. Managed Services: From $1,500/month . Software and usage costs are separate and need checking.

Your next step: bring one workflow you want to improve. We’ll help identify a useful first move. Request a free workflow plan at mainandmachine.com/plan/ , or book a conversation if you prefer.

Illustrative scenario and proposed steps only. No client data or measured results. Scope and pricing require confirmation.

AI Readiness Audit

# Know which AI project is worth building.

The AI Readiness Audit maps how work moves through your business, identifies the useful opportunities, and gives you a phased plan you own. Start with the economics and constraints before committing to a build.
[Discuss your first project →](/book/?service=audit)[Read the sample audit →](/services/sample-audit/)
Free 30-minute AI Opportunity Assessment. We reply within 24 hours.

The engagement At a glance
Fixed price $3,500–$8,500
Timeline 2 to 4 weeks
Deliverable A plan you own
Next step Build, simplify, or wait

What you buy

## A decision document for your operation.

### Map the work as it happens

We look at the handoffs, systems and repeated tasks behind a workflow. The map makes delays and duplicate effort visible before a tool is chosen.

### Rank the useful opportunities

The audit weighs expected benefit against effort, data readiness and the decisions a person needs to own. Estimates are ranges with assumptions, not guaranteed savings.

### Decide what happens next

You leave with an ordered plan and a recommendation about where to start. An audit can support a build, a simpler process change, or a decision to wait.

Representative audit excerpt

### 01 / Intake triage

Current friction : Requests wait in a shared inbox.

First opportunity : Capture details and prepare a routed response.

Next decision : Test with one workflow owner before expanding.

An illustrative workflow, shown in the audit format. Not a client result.
[Read the sample audit](/services/sample-audit/) Included in the agreed scope
- A map of the workflows examined

- A ranked set of opportunities

- Effort and payoff ranges with assumptions

- A phased plan you own outright

Check the fit

## Useful when the problem needs a closer look.

### You know the work is slow, but the first project is unclear

The audit is for established teams with repeated operational work: intake, documents, follow-up, reporting, or information moving between tools. We work with businesses of 5–100 people and $1M–$50M in revenue.

### Bring the people who know the workflow

The useful starting material is the process you run today, examples of the work, the tools involved, and the people responsible for it. Discuss any access or data restrictions in the free assessment before sharing sensitive records.

### Already know what to build?

A paid audit is not a mandatory toll. If your workflow is defined, we can discuss direct [Implementation Sprint scoping](/services/ai-implementation/). If a basic tool or process fix would solve it, a custom build may be unnecessary.

Before commissioning an audit
- Name the operational bottleneck

- Identify the workflow owner

- Describe the systems involved

- Explain data and approval constraints

[Use the readiness checklist →](/guides/ai-readiness-checklist/)

AI Implementation

# Put a defined AI workflow to work.

The AI Implementation Sprint turns an agreed operational problem into a working system: custom agents, automations, or integrations tested in your business and handed to a team trained to run them.
[Scope an implementation →](/book/?service=sprint)[Explore the build catalog →](/services/builds/)
Free 30-minute AI Opportunity Assessment. We reply within 24 hours.

The engagement At a glance
Fixed quote $18,000–$60,000
Timeline 4 to 12 weeks
Ownership Your system
After launch Optional support

Scope before software

## Know what will be built and what it will do.

### Choose a defined workflow

Start with a recurring operational job and a clear owner. Scope the inputs, expected outputs, systems involved and exceptions before work begins. The written quote fixes the scope and price.

### Test inside the real operation

We build against your actual process and test how the system handles ordinary work and the cases that need review. Your team sees the workflow run and learns how to operate it.

### Make the handoff part of the build

A finished sprint includes the working system, its integrations and team training. You own what we build. Ongoing monitoring and maintenance are available separately.

From scope to handoff

### A system your team can run.

- 01 Scope The workflow and acceptance criteria.

- 02 Build Your tools and approval rules, connected.

- 03 Test Normal work, exceptions, and failure cases.

- 04 Handoff Training, documentation, and ownership.

[Inspect a delivered system](/work/marcus/results/) Included in the agreed scope
- Working agents, automations or integrations

- Connections to the systems in scope

- Testing against the operational workflow

- Team training and handoff

Picture the work

## The workflow determines the system.

### An inquiry becomes prepared work

A lead response workflow collects the information your team needs, routes it and prepares the next step. Any automatic replies or actions need explicit boundaries agreed for that build.

### Records move between the right tools

A system connector reduces manual re-entry between the tools you already use. The scope identifies the source of truth, the data that moves, and how exceptions are handled.

### Company knowledge becomes usable

A knowledge base helps people find answers in approved business material. The useful output includes sources a person can check, not simply a fluent answer.

Examples from the catalog
- [Instant Lead Response](/services/builds/instant-lead-response/)

- [Business System Connectors](/services/builds/business-system-connectors/)

- [Company Knowledge Base](/services/builds/company-knowledge-base/)

- Catalog examples show suitability, not promised client results.

[Compare the available builds →](/services/builds/)

Investment and responsibility

## Fixed scope. A written price.

An AI Implementation Sprint is $18,000–$60,000 , quoted fixed before work begins. Typical delivery is 4 to 12 weeks , about 90 days per workflow.
If a scoped workflow is not live in your operation within 90 days, we keep building at no charge until it is.
Your workflow owner helps explain the process, make decisions and review the system in operation. Discuss tool access, data handling, third-party costs and what the agreed scope covers before starting.
If discovery is needed first, the [AI Readiness Audit](/services/ai-readiness-audit/) creates the plan. 100% of your audit fee credits toward a sprint signed within 60 days, up to 25% of the sprint price.

Managed AI Services

# Keep your AI working as the business changes.

Optional Managed Services provides monitoring, maintenance and agreed improvements for systems we built. Your team keeps ownership while we help maintain the workflow as models, vendors and operating needs change.
[Discuss ongoing support →](/book/?service=managed)[See pricing and terms →](/pricing/)
Free 30-minute AI Opportunity Assessment. We reply within 24 hours.

The engagement At a glance
Retainer From $1,500/month
Timeline Ongoing

For Systems we built

What the retainer does

## Keep the working system useful.

### Watch the workflow

Tests and monitoring help identify when a deployed system stops behaving as expected. Your team can flag misses so those examples inform tuning and review.

### Maintain the dependencies

Models, APIs and connected tools change. Maintenance addresses the changes relevant to the systems in your agreed coverage, with testing around the updates.

### Improve what is already running

An agreed block of build time supports new automations and improvements. A plain-language monthly report explains what ran, what was caught and what changed.

Illustrative report format

### Your monthly system review.

Health : Checks, exceptions, and fixes.

Changes : What changed and why.

Next : Agreed priorities for the next month.

A clear record of the systems covered by your agreement.
[Explore testing and monitoring](/services/builds/testing-and-monitoring/) Included in the agreed scope
- Testing and monitoring for deployed systems

- Maintenance as models and vendors change

- Tuning informed by your team’s feedback

- A defined monthly block for improvements

- A one-page monthly report

Decide who will maintain it

## Buy support when it solves a real ownership problem.

### Choose support when your team needs a maintenance partner

Someone needs to own failed runs, tool changes, access and updates. The retainer helps a small team carry that work without leaving every issue with the person whose day job is somewhere else.

### Keep a person accountable inside the business

Your workflow owner remains part of the decision process. They can review the report, flag problems and decide which improvements are worth doing next.

### Run it yourself when that is the better fit

Managed Services is optional. If you have the people and capacity to operate the system, you can do that. The implementation handoff still includes training and ownership.

Agree the boundaries in writing
- The systems covered

- The monitoring and maintenance scope

- The improvement time included

- How your team reports and reviews issues

[Compare support and internal ownership →](/guides/ai-consultant-vs-in-house/)

Pricing and flexibility

## A retainer that can earn its place.

Managed Services starts at From $1,500/month . The quote depends on the systems and coverage agreed. Keep third-party tool and model costs visible alongside the service fee when assessing the total running cost.
No lock-in. Pay annually and the retainer runs 12 months for the price of 10; unused months are refunded if you leave.
We manage systems we built and understand. Your implementation can follow a paid audit or go directly to sprint scoping when the workflow is already defined. A paid audit is not a requirement for every engagement.
The [MARCUS case](/work/marcus/) shows a system built for B:Side Capital, where our founder is CEO. It demonstrates a related-company deployment, not a guaranteed result for every customer.

Fair questions

## How much does AI implementation cost?

01 How much does AI implementation cost for a small business?
The AI Readiness Audit runs $3,500–$8,500 and takes 2 to 4 weeks. An AI Implementation Sprint runs $18,000–$60,000, quoted fixed in writing before work begins. Managed Services runs from $1,500 a month with no lock-in, and a Full Back Office build starts at $95,000. For a practical comparison of scope, pricing models, and total cost, see [What an AI Consultant Costs in 2026](/guides/ai-consultant-cost/); for the monthly costs after the build, see [What AI Automation Costs to Run](/guides/what-ai-automation-costs-to-run/).

02 Is there a guarantee?
Yes, on delivery: if a scoped workflow is not live in your operation within 90 days, we keep building at no charge until it is. The scope is fixed in writing before work begins, so the guarantee is against a spec both sides can read. We do not guarantee ROI numbers — nobody honestly can — but we do guarantee the thing you paid for shows up and runs.

03 Does the audit fee count toward a build?
Yes. 100% of your audit fee credits toward an Implementation Sprint signed within 60 days of the audit, up to 25% of the sprint price. The cap means some audit fees may remain uncredited. Your proposal shows the credit and the remaining amount. The credit is the smaller of your audit fee and one quarter of the sprint price.

04 What does the AI Readiness Audit include?
A workflow map of your real operations, the handful of places AI actually pays, a phased plan you own outright, and a straight read on whether to build at all. It takes 2 to 4 weeks.

05 Why fixed prices instead of hourly?
Because that is how you would want to be treated. The exact price is quoted in writing before work begins and does not move after we start. You will not sit through three discovery calls to learn what something costs. If you are comparing firms, the ten questions in [How to Choose an AI Consultant](/guides/how-to-choose-an-ai-consultant/) include this one — and [a scope a vendor can’t inflate](/guides/how-to-scope-an-ai-project/) keeps the number fixed after you choose.

06 What happens after the 90 days?
Your team is trained to run what we built, and you own all of it. If you want us to keep watching, Managed Services covers monitoring and maintenance as models and vendors shift: from $1,500 a month, cancel any month it stops earning its keep, and pay annually for 12 months at the price of 10. Whether to keep a retainer, name an internal owner, or hire is worked through in [AI Consultant vs. In-House Hire](/guides/ai-consultant-vs-in-house/).

### Want exact numbers?

The free assessment helps establish the right next step. A fixed implementation quote follows an agreed scope; complex work may need a paid audit first.

## Two words. One argument.

We put Main first on purpose. The order is the whole philosophy.

Main the human part

Main Street is the human part. The owner who knows which customer always pays late and which one is worth keeping anyway. The manager who can feel when a week is about to go sideways. The judgment that no model has, and no model will.

Machine the tireless part

The Machine is the other part. It is patient in a way people cannot be. It reads every invoice, watches every queue, drafts the first version at three in the morning, and never gets tired or bored or careless on a Friday afternoon.

& the whole company

The ampersand is the whole company. The machine works for the person: it carries the load the person should not have to carry, and hands every judgment call back to them. The person stays in charge; the software stays in service. Build it in that order and you have built the right thing. That is the only thing we build.

Client story · B:Side Capital

# AI agents that prepare a lender’s back-office work. People own the decisions.

B:Side Capital, an SBA 504 and CDFI lender led by our founder Christopher Myers, needed to reduce repetitive preparation without giving up control of data or decisions. We built MARCUS around its process documents and existing tools: local document processing, filtered model access, and human approval of consequential actions.

[Build something like MARCUS →](/book/)
[See how it works](#solution)

Private by design. Auditable by default. Built from their own process. Published with permission.

Case file : MARCUS · 2026

Client : B:Side Capital

Sector : SBA 504 / CDFI lender

Footprint : 7 departments

The team : 14 AI agents

Runs : Local + hybrid

Updated : July 2026

First 90 days, measured

## What the first 90 days returned.

1,240 hrs

Staff preparation hours returned during the reported 90-day window. This is operating capacity, not measured cash savings.

93 %

Of staff using MARCUS weekly by week six. The public summary does not include the staff denominator.

0

Borrower identifiers reported as sent to outside models during the measurement window. Filtering is required; detection is not guaranteed to be perfect.

100 %

Of consequential actions approved by a person during the reported window, before sending, filing, posting, or paying.

Measurement window: the first 90 days of full-fleet operation. Results are reported by B:Side Capital and reconciled against its audit log, with written approval on file. Preparation time returned is operating capacity, not a claim of reduced payroll. Annualized equivalents are not measured annual savings.

[Read the measured results](/work/marcus/results/)

Who we built it for

Client facts : B:Side

Type : SBA 504 · CDFI

Touches : Borrower financials

Stakes : Regulated · auditable

B:Side Capital is a mission-driven lender, an SBA 504 and CDFI institution whose work touches sensitive borrower financials at every step: intake, eligibility, underwriting support, funding, portfolio monitoring, and the high-stakes work of servicing distressed loans. It’s a business where a single mishandled document isn’t an inconvenience; it’s a compliance event.

Sensitive documents, established processes, and accountable decisions shaped the build from the start.

The problem

## Lending runs on preparation. That’s where the days disappear.

Before anyone can make a decision, someone has to gather the documents, pull the reports, run the checks, and draft the paperwork. The same steps, over and over, across seven departments. That preparation is where the bottlenecks form.

The team needed a defined boundary around borrower documents and a reviewable path from source records to prepared work. Eligibility, credit, and pricing remained with the people responsible for them. The system had to show its sources and record its actions.

The brief, in one line

Take the prep off our people’s plate, without ever taking them out of control.

The solution

## Meet MARCUS.

MARCUS is not an app B:Side’s team had to learn. It’s a colleague that lives inside the tools they already use: Slack, their lending systems, the browser. It does the gathering, checking, and drafting, then hands finished, organized work to a person to approve.

B:Side’s process documentation defined the workflows and the sources each agent should use. That made the work reviewable against the institution’s own operating rules.

Four surfaces the team already knows

01

### A chat front door

Ask a question, get findings back. The way the team already talks to each other.

In Slack

02

### An approval queue

A simple list where a person says yes, sends it back, or escalates.

Human sign-off

03

### A browser assistant

Read-only. Answers questions about the screen in front of you, changes nothing.

On-screen, view-only

04

### The systems of record

Once approved, work lands where it already belongs: their lending platform and tools.

Existing systems

AI agents
: 14
: one for each step of the lending lifecycle

departments
: 7
: from intake to portfolio to distressed-asset servicing

source documents
: ~840
: every action traced to a real B:Side process

Built from their work, not our assumptions

## We didn’t bring a template. We read everything.

Before we wrote a line of code, we reviewed roughly 840 files across every division of the business. From that, we mapped fourteen distinct agents, each one doing a specific, real job, each one citing the exact operations document it came from.

Intake →
Production →
Funding →
Portfolio →
Priority assets →
Across the institution

DEPT 01 Lender Services 2 agents

AGENT 01 Intake agent cited to source

AGENT 02 Eligibility agent cited to source

DEPT 02 Loan Production 4 agents

AGENT 03 Document-prep agent cited to source

AGENT 04 Due-diligence agent cited to source

AGENT 05 Credit-analysis agent cited to source

AGENT 06 Underwriting-support agent cited to source

DEPT 03 Funding 2 agents

AGENT 07 Closing & funding agent cited to source

AGENT 08 Disbursement agent cited to source

DEPT 04 Portfolio 2 agents

AGENT 09 Portfolio-monitoring agent cited to source

AGENT 10 Covenant & reporting agent cited to source

DEPT 05 Priority Assets 2 agents · built last

AGENT 11 Payment-relief agent cited to source

AGENT 12 Loan-resolution agent cited to source

DEPT 06–07 Sales & Administration 2 agents · cross-cutting

AGENT 13 Outreach & pipeline agent cited to source

AGENT 14 Compliance & audit agent cited to source

Every step in the blueprint cites the operations document it came from. That’s the difference between an AI demo and an AI system.

How it was built

We built it the way you’d actually want a system this consequential built: in order, one capability at a time, each piece proven on real files before the next one shipped.

Highest exposure, built last

The most delicate work, payment relief and loan resolution, was deliberately built last, once trust in the system was already established.

The local processing path

## Local processing. Defined data boundaries.

MARCUS processes borrower documents on a secured machine in B:Side’s own server closet. A privacy filter scans prompts and documents before model processing. Selected tasks can use a commercial model on filtered text, as described in the [results and architecture detail](/work/marcus/results/).

L1

### Local by default

Borrower-document processing runs on B:Side’s hardware. External model use is a separate routing decision for selected tasks on filtered text; local deployment does not make every downstream service local.

L2

### Identifiers filtered before model processing

Microsoft Presidio detects supported identifiers for removal before model processing. Detection is imperfect; seeded tests, routing limits, and review are part of the control.

L3

### Encrypted and tamper-evident

Stored documents and work products are encrypted. Actions are recorded in an append-only, hash-chained log so changes to recorded entries can be checked.

B:Side server closet On-prem

#### Borrower document

raw · sensitive · stays put

↓ Presidio detects and removes identifiers

#### Local model

processes filtered text

↓ encrypt + log to chain

#### Encrypted store & audit chain

append-only · tamper-evident

⛌ Local document-processing path shown. Selected external tasks use filtered text.

The diagram shows the local processing path. Read the [security review](/security/) for deployment choices, filter limitations, and the questions to ask about your own workflow.

One rule behind everything

## MARCUS prepares the work. People decide.

Consequential sending, filing, posting, and paying require a person’s approval. MARCUS does not decide eligibility, credit, or price. Those numbers come from systems, never from memory. Every request arrives the same way.

STEP 01

### It shows its work

Here’s what I did, here’s what I’m asking for, here’s the source I relied on.

STEP 02

### A person chooses

Approve it, send it back with comments, or escalate it. While a request waits, nothing moves.

STEP 03

### It escalates, never proceeds

If it waits too long, it escalates to a person automatically. It never proceeds on its own.

#### Numbers come from systems

Eligibility, credit, and price are looked up, never recalled from memory.

#### Every step is logged

Attributable and auditable, down to the source document.

#### It’s the design, not a limit

Humans in control isn’t a constraint we worked around. It’s the point.

What changed

## B:Side’s people get their day back for the work only people can do.

With the preparation handled, the team is free for the relationships, the customer service, and the judgment calls that actually move a deal. The repetitive prep that used to create bottlenecks now arrives finished, organized, and named the way the team already does it, ready for a human to review.

The result is an institution that moves faster without giving up an ounce of control, compliance, or trust.

If the stakes are real

MARCUS is what Main & Machine builds when the stakes are real: private, auditable, built from your own processes, and designed so your people stay in control the whole way through. Builds in this class are published on the price list as [The Full Back Office](/pricing/#backoffice) — from $95,000, four taken per year. The operating design

## Prepare the work. Keep the decision.

MARCUS connects the records, communication tools, and books B:Side already uses. The machine prepares; a person reviews consequential work before it moves.

Architecture illustration, not a product screenshot. B:Side owns the server used for local processing. Selected tasks can use external reasoning on filtered text. The filter is a required processing step, not a guarantee that every identifier is detected.

[Open the full system map](/images/diagrams/marcus-workflow.svg)

- Prepare safely. Requests and records pass through the privacy filter to a local model or selected external reasoning on filtered text.

- Bring the evidence. Prepared work includes sources and exceptions for the reviewer.

- A person decides. Approve, send back, or escalate. Consequential action follows approval.

Why it was built in this order B:Side already had the data, the front door, and the books — process documents by the hundred, a team living in Slack, systems of record for loans and accounting. What they didn’t have was a way to ask any of it a question, or a way to hand it the preparation work, without borrower data leaving a controlled environment.
So we built the seven things below, in order, each one proven on real files before the next shipped. The highest-exposure work — funds movement, distressed assets — was deliberately built last, behind the strictest gates, once trust was established.

Sources and limits

## How to read the results.

Use these figures to understand one deployment. A comparable result in your business needs its own baseline, scope, and measurement.

[Download the public evidence brief](/work/marcus/results/evidence.txt) · [Build your own workflow measurement log](/blog/how-to-measure-ai-roi/)

Period and publication : The first 90 days of full-fleet operation, published July 31, 2026. The server was commissioned in February 2026. Exact measurement start and end dates are not published here.

Source and approval : B:Side reports the figures and reconciled them against its audit log. Christopher Myers signed off in his roles at both organizations; written approval is on file. This is not an independent audit.

Preparation time : The preparation-time figure measures returned capacity during the stated window. Annualizing it assumes a similar workload and rate of time returned throughout the year. That would be an estimate, not measured annual savings or a claim of reduced payroll.

Adoption and review : Weekly adoption measures staff use by week six. Human approval covers consequential actions during the reported window. The staff denominator and underlying time-study baseline are not included in this public summary.

Data handling : Source documents are processed locally. Selected tasks can use external reasoning on filtered text. The external-identifier figure describes reported exposure during this window; a mandatory filter does not guarantee perfect detection. [Read the deployment controls and limitations](/security/).

Comparison with your business : Include review time, exceptions, operating costs, and the useful work returned capacity would support. [Discuss the evidence and assumptions](/book/?service=sprint) before using these figures in an investment decision.

The implementation record

## Explore the work behind the figures.

Open a chapter for the delivered components, reported measurements, and operating boundaries.

01 Prepare from company records Server · filtering · knowledge

Private AI server
B:Side owns the hardware used for local model processing and can maintain or replace the model independently of the workflow.

### One box, in a locked room, with B:Side’s name on the invoice.

We specified and configured a server to run open-source models locally. The hardware was purchased in B:Side’s name at cost, with zero markup. This gave the team ownership of the local processing environment.

We have already swapped the local model once for a newer one — better answers, same workflows, nobody retrained. Once the machine is yours and the filter is in place, the model is just a part you replace.

99.96 %

Uptime since commissioning in February 2026 — one planned maintenance window, zero unplanned outages.

2.1M

Local model calls processed on B:Side’s hardware during the reported 90-day window. Selected external-model tasks are a separate processing route.

$0

Hardware markup. The server was bought at cost in the client’s name.

1

Mid-flight model upgrade, completed in an evening, with zero workflow changes for staff.

Ownership: B:Side owns the server. Hardware, configuration, and ongoing care are separate parts of evaluating a comparable deployment.

Data privacy filter
Staff needed a controlled route for using models with company information, rather than choosing a public chatbot independently.

### A privacy filter before model processing.

Prompts and attachments pass through a filter that detects and removes supported personal identifiers. Tasks can then route to a local model or, by B:Side’s choice, to a commercial model on filtered text. Mandatory filtering establishes the route; it does not guarantee every identifier was detected.

We don’t take the filter’s accuracy on faith. A seeded set of documents carrying known, planted identifiers runs against it every month — and every miss becomes a new test case.

Routine work can use the local model while selected tasks use external reasoning on filtered text. External processing remains a data-handling decision. The recall result below describes the seeded test set, not a guarantee of perfect detection in every production document.

100 %

Of prompts and attachments cleared the filter before reaching any model. No bypass path exists in the architecture.

1.9M

Personal identifiers detected and stripped — names, SSNs, account numbers — across ~38,000 documents processed.

99.8 %

Detection recall on the monthly seeded test set. This measures known test identifiers, not every possible identifier in production.

0

PII incidents reported since the filter went live.

Data boundary: Review which tasks can use external models, what text they receive, and how filtering is tested before choosing a deployment.

Company knowledge base
The company remembers more than any one person in it. This is where that memory went so it could be asked questions.

### Everything B:Side knows, in one place, in a form the machine can use.

Structured loan records on one side; process documents, correspondence, and policies on the other — joined so a single question can cross both. A lender has loans and findings the way a contractor has jobs and change orders: same shape, different nouns.

B:Side defined the core records, events, document sources, and access rules in a knowledge-base questionnaire. Those answers guided the tables, indexes, ingestion pipeline, and read tools. The reported delivery time below starts from the completed questionnaire.

2 wks

From completed questionnaire to a queryable knowledge base — generated from the intake, not hand-designed.

~840

Process documents ingested, joined with thousands of loan records and a decade of institutional correspondence.

1,200 /mo

Questions asked by staff by month three — the questions that used to wait for whoever just knows.

96 %

Of answers delivered with a citation to the source document or record. The rest say they do not know, and escalate to a person.

Dependencies: The knowledge base depends on useful source records and defined access rules. Start by identifying which questions it must answer and which sources are authoritative.

02 Deliver into the team’s day Slack · workspace · accounting

Where the work arrives
The best interface is the one their people were already staring at.

### No new app. No new login. The first question came eleven minutes after go-live.

MARCUS works inside B:Side’s Slack, where staff already communicate. Prepared work and approvals arrive in the same channels, reducing the need to switch tools to review a task.

Each division received a short introduction to the workflow. Familiar tools reduced interface training; staff still needed to understand what the system prepared, what to check, and when to escalate.

11 min

From go-live to the first real staff question, before the introductory session.

93 %

Weekly active adoption by week six, across all seven divisions — including the skeptics.

71 %

Of all MARCUS interactions happen in Slack — finished work delivered to the channel where the team already works.

Adoption: Put prepared work where staff already work, then measure whether they use it and how often it needs correction.

A workspace of their own
A company chat workspace connected to approved records and the same filtering and routing controls.

### A branded workspace for everyone who just wants to ask something.

Slack is for teams who want finished work delivered to them. The chat workspace is for the other moments — drafting, summarizing, looking something up — connected to the knowledge base, running on B:Side’s server, behind B:Side’s filter. Staff opened it the way they would open any chat tool, because that is exactly what it looks like.

In week two, a question about historical loans exposed the need to connect the knowledge base. The interface alone could not answer a question about records it could not access. That shaped the next integration step.

380 /wk

Conversations per week by month three — policy lookups, document summaries, and first drafts leading the mix.

100 %

Of chat traffic routed through the privacy filter in the reported deployment.

Wk 2

When the first question about loan history identified a need to connect the knowledge base.

Scope: The chat interface, company knowledge, and model hosting are related components. A useful scope states what information is connected and who can access it.

Connected to the books
The books already knew the answer. This is what it took to ask.

### Reconciliation prepared. Invoices staged. Receivables chased. Nothing posted until a person approves.

The accounting connector let MARCUS see the books: month-end reconciliation arrives prepared with exceptions flagged, vendor invoices arrive pre-coded with the source attached, aging receivables get follow-ups drafted the day they cross the threshold. A person approves every entry before anything posts — that is not a limitation, it is the design.

The connector prepares work against B:Side’s existing accounting records. The review remains with the person responsible for the books, with sources and exceptions available before anything posts.

Month-end reconciliation prep

before · ~2.5 days

after · ~3 hrs of review

Eligibility pre-check turnaround

before · 2–3 days

after · same morning

504 package assembly

before · ~6.5 hrs

after · ~40-min review

Bar lengths are proportional to time. “After” figures are human review time — the preparation itself happens before anyone sits down.

640

Vendor invoices staged in 90 days, each pre-coded with source attached — every one approved by a person before posting.

41

Reconciliation mismatches surfaced automatically before month-end — found by the system, decided by a person.

−9 days

Improvement in average days-to-collect on fee invoices, from follow-ups drafted the day an invoice ages past threshold.

Integration: A comparable build starts with your accounting and operating systems. The [build catalog](/services/builds/) describes capabilities that can be included in a scoped engagement.

03 Keep decisions accountable Testing · approval · escalation

Proof it still works
Anyone can demo an AI. We show ours failing, on purpose, on a schedule.

### Test the exceptions before they reach the team.

Nightly tests exercise B:Side’s configuration against eligibility edge cases, malformed documents, planted identifiers, and adversarial prompts. The results appear on a dashboard the team can review. The reported regression count below describes issues caught during the measurement period; tests cannot establish that every possible failure has been covered.

An append-only, hash-chained log records system actions. It helps the team trace an action to its trigger, source, and approval, and check recorded entries for changes.

2,100

Automated assertions run nightly against the production configuration — plus a monthly deliberate failure drill.

47

Regressions caught by the harness before any staff member encountered them. Zero found by staff first.

3.4M

Entries on the tamper-evident audit log — every action traceable to its trigger, its approver, and its source document.

84 %

Of the test harness consists of reusable assertion-running code; the remainder consists of client-specific test cases.

After launch: A test suite and audit trail ship with the build. Optional Managed Services adds ongoing monitoring and maintenance of the agreed systems.

One rule behind everything

### MARCUS prepares the work. People decide.

Consequential sending, filing, posting, and payments wait for human approval. Routine routing and escalation follow the agreed rules.

MARCUS never decides eligibility, credit, or price — those numbers come from systems, never from memory. Across the measurement window, every consequential action passed through a human approval: approve, send back, or escalate.

Escalation is automatic, including for anything that has waited too long. Silence never means yes.

Approve
89 %

The work moves forward — approved on first presentation, most within the hour.

Send back
9 %

Returned with comments. Every send-back becomes training signal and, where it generalizes, a new test case.

Escalate
2 %

Handed to the right person, plus every request that waited too long. Escalation is automatic; silence never means yes.

- [Main & Machine](/)

- Security & data handling

Security & data handling

# Know where your data goes. Know who stays in control.

Review the deployment, data handling, and approval controls before you commit. These are the controls used in MARCUS, the system running at B:Side Capital, and the questions we work through for your own build. Your written scope identifies the deployment and controls that apply to your workflow.

The architecture In production

Models Local-first

PII Filtered pre-model

Storage Encrypted at rest

Audit log Append-only chain

Actions Defined approvals

01 / The controls

## Five controls, in the order your data meets them.

A useful security review follows the data: where it enters, what the model receives, where results are stored, and who can authorize an action. Deployment choices belong in that review before work begins.

C-01

### Local models, on your hardware.

For regulated workflows, local models can run on hardware you own. In MARCUS, borrower documents are processed locally; selected tasks can route filtered text to a commercial model. When external processing is appropriate, the data boundary and trade-off are described in the written quote for you to decide.

Deployment: on-prem by default for regulated data

C-02

### Personal information is filtered before model processing.

Microsoft Presidio detects supported personal identifiers such as names, Social Security numbers, and account numbers so they can be removed before model processing. Automated detection can miss information. The filter is one control alongside deployment restrictions, access decisions, and tests using known identifiers. [Read Presidio’s documented limitations](https://github.com/microsoft/presidio/blob/main/docs/faq.md).

Engine: Microsoft Presidio · runs before model ingestion

C-03

### Stored documents and work products are encrypted.

MARCUS encrypts stored documents, extracted data, and work products. Encryption helps protect stored information; access to the running system and its keys still matters. Review those responsibilities as part of your deployment.

Scope: all stored documents and derived data

C-04

### Every action writes to an append-only, tamper-evident log.

MARCUS records actions in an append-only, hash-chained audit log. The chain makes changes to recorded entries detectable when verified. It provides evidence for a review; it does not replace access control, retention decisions, or an investigation of the underlying action.

Property: append-only · chained · verifiable

C-05

### A person signs off on every consequential action.

Consequential actions require human approval. In MARCUS, financial and lending work is prepared for a person to approve, return, or escalate. A customer-facing workflow may handle routine replies or bookings within its agreed scope. The scope must distinguish those actions from decisions that wait for approval.

Rule: the machine prepares; people decide

02 / Before you approve a build

## Bring these questions to the review.

- Deployment. Which work stays local, which can use external services, and what information can cross that boundary?

- Access. Who can read the records, administer the system, approve actions, and revoke access?

- Retention. Where are source files, work products, backups, and audit records kept?

- Decisions. What can run automatically, what needs a person, and where does an exception go?

- Evidence. What is tested, how are failures reported, and what does an audit-log review establish?

- Responsibilities. Which controls belong to your team, to Main & Machine, and to a third-party provider?

03 / Not a policy document

## This architecture is running right now.

MARCUS supports B:Side Capital, a regulated SBA 504 / CDFI lender led by our founder: 14 AI agents across 7 departments, built from ~840 source documents. It combines local processing, a privacy filter, an audit trail, and human approval of consequential actions. The published results report borrower identifiers sent to an outside model: 0 during the reported measurement window. [Read the results and their limits](/work/marcus/results/).

[Read the MARCUS case study](/work/marcus/)

Have a security questionnaire? Send it, or bring your IT reviewer to the free 30-minute assessment. The person answering is the founder who is accountable for the build — and “that control doesn’t apply to your workflow” is an answer we’ll put in writing too. The plain-English version of the cloud-versus-on-prem call is in [where your AI data actually goes](/guides/ai-data-cloud-vs-on-prem/).

[Book the free assessment →](/book/)

The guarantee: If a scoped workflow is not live in your operation within 90 days, we keep building at no charge until it is.

The credit: 100% of your audit fee credits toward a sprint signed within 60 days, up to 25% of the sprint price.

[See the price list →](/pricing/)

Fair questions

## What compliance asks.

### Something we didn’t cover?

Ask it directly. Security questions land with the founder, not a sales queue.

[Ask a security question](/contact/)

01 Does our data leave our building?
It depends on the agreed deployment. Local processing can keep source documents on your hardware; selected tasks may use external models on filtered text. We describe external processing in the written quote so you can review the data boundary before work begins.

02 Do AI models see our customers’ personal information?
A privacy filter detects and removes supported identifiers before processing. Automated detection is imperfect, so we review the data, deployment restrictions, and additional controls for the workflow. Passing a document through a filter is not a guarantee that every identifier was removed.

03 How is stored data protected?
MARCUS encrypts stored documents and work products and records actions in an append-only, hash-chained audit log. Your deployment review should also cover access, keys, backups, and retention.

04 Can we audit what the system did?
Yes. An append-only, hash-chained log records system actions and supports checking for changes to recorded entries. Your review should establish who can access the log, how it is retained, and how verification is performed.

05 Can the AI act on its own?
The scope defines that boundary. Routine replies and bookings can run within agreed rules; consequential actions require approval. MARCUS prepares financial and lending work for people to review and uses systems of record for eligibility, credit, and price inputs.

06 Has this architecture run in a regulated environment?
Yes. MARCUS supports B:Side Capital, a regulated SBA 504 / CDFI lender led by our founder, with 14 AI agents across 7 departments. The case is published with permission. Its controls and reported results are evidence of that deployment, not a certification of every future build.

Read next A plain-English walkthrough of this architecture, with the production figures behind it: [private AI for small business](/guides/private-ai-for-small-business/).

Law, accounting, insurance and advisory firms of twelve to eighty people, concentrated downtown, in the Tech Center and along the Boulder corridor. The Field Guide / 01

# What an AI consultant costs in 2026.

[Christopher Myers](/about/) — Founder, Main & Machine Updated September 2026

What you buy matters more than the billing label. Compare our published prices, see what a useful quote includes, and budget for the work after launch.

Field Guide No. 01

Reading time 4 min

Compare Scope + total cost

Our range $3,500–$60,000

## What does an AI consultant cost in 2026?

There is no useful single rate for advice, a working automation, and a whole back office. Price the deliverable first. At Main & Machine, an [AI Readiness Audit](/services/ai-readiness-audit/) is $3,500–$8,500 over 2 to 4 weeks; an [AI Implementation Sprint](/services/ai-implementation/) is $18,000–$60,000 over 4 to 12 weeks. We agree the scope and quote a fixed price in writing before work begins.

Those are our published prices, not a survey of the market. Use the questions below to compare any proposal, including ours. Two quotes are only comparable when they promise the same work.

## How should you compare an hourly quote with a fixed price?

Ask for three numbers: the rate, the estimated hours, and the spending limit. Then ask what happens at the limit. A rate alone cannot tell you the project cost; a fixed price alone cannot tell you what is included.

Hourly work can make sense for investigation or a changing backlog. A fixed price is useful once the workflow, dependencies, and acceptance criteria are clear. In either case, put the deliverables, review points, and approval for additional work in writing. The contract matters more than the billing label.

## What should an implementation quote include?

A working system needs more than a demonstration. Ask what it will read, what it will produce, which tools it will touch, and what happens when it cannot finish. Then check who tests it, who approves it, and who can run it after handoff.

Compare
Get this in writing
Why it changes the price

: Workflow : Trigger, input, output, owner, and explicit exclusions : One clear handoff is different from a whole department.

: Connections : Systems, access permissions, data quality, and API limits : Missing access or inconsistent records can change the work.

: Testing : Representative cases, exception handling, and acceptance criteria : A demo is not evidence that your normal workload will run.

: Handoff : Ownership, documentation, training, credentials, and dependencies : Your team needs a system it can operate and maintain.

: After launch : Tool costs, usage assumptions, monitoring, and support terms : The build price is only one part of the operating cost.

: Changes : How new requirements are assessed and approved : A fixed scope still needs a clear way to handle new work.

Take this comparison to every seller. Leave a cell blank when the proposal does not answer it; do not fill it with an assumption.

## When is a paid audit worth buying?

When the uncertainty is consequential: nobody has measured the manual work, the systems disagree, the data needs investigation, or several workflows compete for the first build. An audit should help you choose, including a decision to simplify the process or wait.

If the workflow is already defined and can be scoped, you can go directly from the free assessment to a written sprint quote. The audit is not a toll booth. [Read the illustrative sample audit](/services/sample-audit/) to see the decision it should support.

Scoping is worth taking seriously. [RAND’s interviews with 65 experienced AI practitioners](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2680-1.html) identified misunderstood problems, missing data, technology-first decisions, inadequate infrastructure, and technical limits as recurring causes of project failure. A low price does not resolve any of those.

## What are Main & Machine’s published prices?

- AI Readiness Audit: $3,500–$8,500; 2 to 4 weeks. A workflow map, opportunity assessment, and phased plan you own.

- AI Implementation Sprint: $18,000–$60,000; 4 to 12 weeks. A defined system, tested in your operation and handed to your team.

- Managed Services: from $1,500 a month. Optional support for the system after launch, with no lock-in.

- The Full Back Office: from $95,000. A separate multi-department engagement over one to two quarters; four taken per year.

The [full price list](/pricing/) explains the inclusions and terms. If a scoped workflow is not live in your operation within 90 days, we keep building at no charge until it is. That is a delivery guarantee, not a promised return on investment.

## How much should you budget for the first year?

At our prices, an audit plus one sprint totals $21,500–$68,500 before the audit credit and ongoing costs . If discovery is unnecessary, budget for the sprint alone. 100% of your audit fee credits toward a sprint signed within 60 days, up to 25% of the sprint price.

For example, an $8,500 audit followed by an $18,000 sprint receives a $4,500 credit because of the cap. The combined fees are $22,000 before ongoing costs. A $3,500 audit followed by the same sprint receives the full $3,500 credit if the sprint is signed within 60 days.

Add the [monthly tools and model usage](/guides/what-ai-automation-costs-to-run/), any hardware, your team’s review time, and optional maintenance. Our $50–$500 monthly planning band covers typical small-business tools and model usage; it does not include the build, hardware, internal labor, or Managed Services. Ask for the assumptions behind your own estimate.

Then test the value at a conservative level of adoption. Time returned is capacity; it becomes cash savings only when a cost actually falls. [Work through the ROI math](/guides/ai-roi-math-small-business/), use the [calculator](/calculator/) as a starting model, and take the [20-point readiness checklist](/guides/ai-readiness-checklist/) before committing.

Price basis. Main & Machine prices are published first-party offers. The worked credit calculation is illustrative. No competitor minimums, industry averages, or guaranteed payback are asserted here.

The Field Guide / 02

# The AI readiness checklist: 20 points.

[Christopher Myers](/about/) — Founder, Main & Machine Updated September 2026

Run it in an afternoon, without hiring anyone — including us. Twenty checks across your workflows, data, team, and economics, with scoring bands that include the answer nobody sells: wait.

Field Guide No. 02

Reading time 6 min

Checks 20

Cost to run $0

Automated version AI-Ready Score

## What makes a business ready for AI?

Documented workflows, data somebody can actually export, one named person with time to review what a machine produces, and a number on what the manual work costs you. That is the whole secret — not a data science team, not a bigger budget, not a platform migration.

The twenty checks below test exactly those four things. They are the same questions we ask in the first week of a paid [AI Readiness Audit](/services/ai-readiness-audit/), published here because you can run most of them yourself. A business that passes fifteen of these will get more from a $18,000 build than an unprepared one gets from a $200,000 engagement.

## How do you use this checklist?

Score one point for every item you can check off without squinting, zero for the rest — no half points. Twenty minutes if you know your business; an afternoon if you have to go look, and having to go look is itself a finding.

Be strict. The checklist only helps if the score is true, and nobody is watching you take it. If an item makes you say “sort of,” that is a zero with better posture.

## Are your workflows ready? (Points 1–5)

Ready means known, written down, and owned. AI automates what you can describe; it cannot automate a vibe.

- You can name your three most repetitive workflows without checking. If you have to ask a manager, start there — the asking is the audit.

- At least one of those workflows is written down, step by step, somewhere other than someone’s head. A checklist, a wiki page, even a dusty SOP. Machines learn from documents, not folklore.

- You know roughly how often each one runs. Ten times a week or ten times a day changes what a fix is worth by an order of magnitude.

- You can describe the exceptions. Someone can say what the weird ten percent looks like — the rush order, the disputed invoice, the client who calls instead of emailing.

- Each workflow has one owner with a name. “Operations handles that” is not a name. Automation without an owner is a stray dog.

## Is your data ready? (Points 6–10)

Ready does not mean clean — nobody’s data is clean. It means you know where each fact lives and you can get it out.

- You can say which system is the truth for each core fact. Customer, order, invoice, job status: one home each. Two systems that disagree is the most expensive kind of normal.

- No critical number lives only in a spreadsheet on one person’s desktop. If payroll week depends on Carol’s laptop surviving, fix that before any AI conversation.

- You can export your own data without calling a vendor. Try it this week. A system that holds your data hostage will hold your automation hostage too.

- You know what you are obliged to keep private, and for whom. Clients, patients, employees — the obligations differ, and the build must honor them. Where data may and may not go is the subject of [Where Your Data Goes](/blog/where-your-data-goes/).

- Someone can pull last month’s numbers in under an hour, without IT. If a basic report takes a week, the machine will automate confusion at scale.

## Is your team ready? (Points 11–15)

Most AI projects fail on people, not technology. These five checks find out before the invoice does.

- Someone at the top actually wants this. A sponsor who will spend attention on it — not an owner who merely tolerates the experiment.

- A specific person has two to three hours a week to review what the system drafts. Every system worth building routes judgment to a human. That human needs a calendar, not a title.

- Your team has survived a process change in the past year. New POS, new scheduling tool, new anything. If the last change died in quiet mutiny, the pattern will repeat.

- You can name who says “stop.” When the machine misbehaves, one person has the authority to pull the cord and the standing to be believed.

- Training sticks here. Your people have learned a tool before and still used it in month three. Software that nobody opens is furniture.

## Are your economics ready? (Points 16–20)

AI is an investment with a payback period, not a lottery ticket. These checks confirm you can do the arithmetic — because a vendor certainly will not do it against themselves.

- You know what an hour of admin work costs you, fully loaded. Wage plus taxes plus benefits. Every automation case is built on this number.

- You can name the three workflows that cost the most. Not the most annoying — the most expensive. They are frequently not the same list.

- You have a budget range, even a soft one. For scale: our audits run $3,500–$8,500 and sprints $18,000–$60,000, fixed in writing. If those numbers are unthinkable, the answer is “not yet,” and that is a fine answer.

- You expect ranges, not guarantees. Anyone who promises exact ROI is selling something other than results. We publish [our assumptions](/calculator/); a promise dressed as a number is a red flag.

- You are willing to stop a failing project at day 45. Not day 300. The discipline to quit early is worth more than the discipline to start.

## How do you score it?

Use these bands as discussion prompts, not a validated readiness test. Sixteen or more suggests a useful scoping conversation. Ten to fifteen suggests resolving the failed checks before committing. Nine or fewer suggests preparation first. A critical issue with data access, approval, or ownership can outweigh the total. The long version of “wait” — the signs themselves, and a 90-day plan that costs almost nothing — is in [Signs You Are Not Ready for AI](/guides/signs-you-are-not-ready-for-ai/).

One pattern is worth naming because it is so common: a business that scores eighteen on workflows and economics but fails points 11 through 15 — the team section. That firm will buy a good system and starve it, because nobody has the hours to review what it drafts. If your zeros cluster in one section, fix that section before anything else; a lopsided score fails in more expensive ways than a low one.

Waiting is not falling behind. Most of what a low score reveals — an undocumented workflow, a hostage export, a missing owner — costs little or nothing to fix and pays off whether or not you ever build. The items in the data section are the usual culprits, and most are a policy decision, not a purchase. Fix the foundations, retake the list in a quarter, and you will have gained ground on competitors who bought first and prepared never. When you do take meetings, bring the [ten vetting questions](/guides/how-to-choose-an-ai-consultant/), and know [how to compare proposals](/guides/ai-consultant-cost/) before anyone quotes you.

## Is there an automated version?

Yes — the [AI-Ready Score](/score/): fourteen questions, about seven minutes, and you get a 0–100 score plus the one constraint to fix first. No sales call follows it.

We built it as the instrumented version of this page. The checklist tells you what to look at; the Score weighs the answers the way we would in an audit and hands you a number you can retake next quarter. Run both — the gap between your self-score here and your Score there is usually the most instructive number of all.

Fair questions

## About AI readiness.

### Want the numbers?

The full price list is published — audits, sprints, managed services, all on one page.

[Read the price list →](/pricing/)

01 How do I know if my business is ready for AI? +
Run the 20 checks on this page: documented workflows, exportable data, a named owner with review time, and a number on what the manual work costs. Sixteen or more and you are ready to build; nine or fewer means fix the foundations first.

02 What should be in place before hiring an AI consultant? +
At minimum: your three most repetitive workflows named, one of them written down, a person with two to three hours a week to review outputs, and a budget range. Those four save you money in week one of any engagement.

03 Do I need clean data before starting with AI? +
No — nobody's data is clean. You need to know which system is the truth for each core fact and be able to export it without calling a vendor. That is a policy decision more often than a purchase.

04 Is there a free automated readiness assessment? +
Yes — the AI-Ready Score: fourteen questions, about seven minutes, a 0–100 score, and the one constraint to fix first. No sales call follows it.

The Field Guide / 04

# How to choose an AI consultant.

[Christopher Myers](/about/) — Founder, Main & Machine Updated September 2026

Ten questions that separate builders from hype merchants. Ask every firm all ten — including us. The good ones answer in plain English; the rest answer in adjectives.

Field Guide No. 04

Reading time 6 min

Questions 10

Applies to Us included

## How do you choose an AI consultant?

Ask every candidate the same ten questions and write down what you can verify. Start with scope, accountable people, data handling, proof, and the cost after launch. A missing answer is something to resolve before signing, not something to fill with optimism.

They are drawn from the same standard we publish against ourselves — the “what we don’t promise” list on [our method page](/method/). Print this page and bring it to every meeting, ours included. If our answers and this list ever disagree, that is your red flag.

## The ten questions

Each comes with what a good answer contains — and what a bad one sounds like.

Run the meeting the same way every time: same questions, same order, answers written down. Comparing firms only works when the inputs match, and taking notes changes the answers you get — vague firms get specific or get visibly uncomfortable, and both are information.

### 1. What will this cost, and when do I learn the exact number?

Ask for a useful range before buying discovery, and find out what must be learned before the final quote. Our audit is $3,500–$8,500 and our sprint is $18,000–$60,000. We fix the scoped price in writing before work begins. [Guide 01](/guides/ai-consultant-cost/) shows how to compare deliverables, exclusions, and ongoing costs.

Bad answer: “We cannot tell you what discovery delivers or what it costs.”

### 2. Will you guarantee an ROI number?

This one is a trap, and the right answer is no. Real results depend on your execution, so a serious firm quotes ranges and shows its assumptions; a firm that guarantees “300% ROI” is quoting fiction with confidence. We publish [the assumptions behind our estimates](/calculator/) precisely so nobody has to take a promise on faith.

Bad answer: “Clients typically see 10x returns in 90 days, guaranteed.”

### 3. How long until something actually works?

Ask for the stages, dependencies, and acceptance criteria behind the date. Our sprints typically take 4 to 12 weeks; a separate audit takes 2 to 4 weeks when needed. A simple integration may be faster than a multi-system document workflow. The useful answer explains what has to be ready, not just when the demo will run.

Bad answer: “We can have you fully AI-powered in two weeks.”

### 4. Who scopes the project, and who builds it?

Ask who is accountable for the scope, who implements it, who reviews the work, and who signs off. Those can be different people; the responsibilities should be clear. At Main & Machine, Christopher owns scoping and sign-off, supported by the build team. [Meet the founder and see the delivery roles](/about/).

Bad answer: “You will find out who owns delivery after signing.”

### 5. Will you tell me if AI is wrong for us right now?

“Wait a quarter” must be an answer the firm can afford to give, or every diagnosis will be “build.” Ask when they last told a prospect not to buy. A firm whose audit can conclude “don’t build yet, and here’s why, in writing” is scoping for your benefit, not their pipeline.

Bad answer: “Every business needs AI today — the risk is waiting.”

### 6. What tools will you recommend, and what do you earn from them?

Ask which alternatives were considered and whether commissions, referral fees, or platform requirements influence the recommendation. A useful answer explains why the tool fits your workflow and what it will cost to leave. Our method includes recommending a free tool when it is sufficient.

Bad answer: “Our partner status is the reason this is the right tool for you.”

### 7. Where does our data go?

Ask which records leave your systems, where they are processed, who can access them, and how long they are retained. Our published [MARCUS](/work/marcus/) case processes borrower documents locally and can use external reasoning on filtered text for selected tasks. The [security page](/security/) explains filter and log limitations. Request the same specificity for your proposed build.

Bad answer: “It’s all encrypted in the cloud, totally secure.”

### 8. Who can overrule the system?

Name a person with authority to stop the system, and agree which actions may run automatically. Consequential decisions need an explicit approval path; routine replies or data movements may use defined rules. Ask how exceptions are surfaced and how the team resumes manual work when needed.

Bad answer: “The beauty is it runs itself — no oversight needed.”

### 9. What do we own when you leave?

Ask exactly what transfers: custom code, configuration, prompts, documentation, credentials, and data. Identify third-party licenses and services that remain subscriptions. Our sprint includes ownership of what we build and team training; the scope should make the handoff and ongoing dependencies clear.

Bad answer: “Most clients stay on our platform long-term.”

### 10. Show me something you built.

Ask for a working example, its starting problem, the delivered scope, and the evidence behind the results. Our public case is [MARCUS](/work/marcus/), built for B:Side Capital where our founder is CEO. That affiliation matters. The [results page](/work/marcus/results/) explains the measurement window and limits; the [illustrative sample audit](/services/sample-audit/) shows the planning artifact. Ask each firm what is actual client evidence and what is an example.

Bad answer: “We’ve delivered AI transformation for leading brands across verticals.”

## What are the red flags, in one list?

Pause on guaranteed returns without a defensible basis, unidentified delivery owners, unexplained data handling, hidden recurring costs, and unverifiable proof. A short timeline, a paid discovery phase, or a platform partnership is not automatically wrong; an inability to explain its fit is the problem.

A pilot needs a decision at the end: expand, revise, or stop. Ask which cases it will test, who accepts the result, and how the production costs differ. Our sprint is a scoped implementation, not an open-ended sequence of pilots.

The practical defense is a written comparison. Keep the same questions and evidence standards for every candidate. The Ampersand essay [How to Smell the Hype](/blog/how-to-smell-the-hype/) develops the same skeptical habit.

## Why publish questions we could fail?

Because we would rather be disqualified by a sharp buyer than hired by a confused one. A client who chose us against a real standard stays; a client who was dazzled churns — so the standard is good business, not virtue.

It is also the standard we already signed. Our [method page](/method/) lists what we promise and what we refuse to promise, and this guide is that list turned into questions anyone can ask any firm. Use it on us first: book the [free 30-minute assessment](/book/) and ask all ten. If you are still comparing, [Guide 01 compares scope and total cost](/guides/ai-consultant-cost/) and [Guide 03 runs the hire-or-engage math](/guides/ai-consultant-vs-in-house/). Once you choose, two companions keep the engagement straight: [a scope a vendor can’t inflate](/guides/how-to-scope-an-ai-project/), and [exactly what an audit should hand you](/guides/what-is-an-ai-readiness-audit/).

Fair questions

## Vetting an AI consultant.

### Want the numbers?

The full price list is published — audits, sprints, managed services, all on one page.

[Read the price list →](/pricing/)

01 What should I ask an AI consultant before hiring them? +
Ten questions: the exact cost and when you learn it, whether they guarantee ROI (they should not), the real timeline, who scopes versus who builds, whether they can say wait, tool incentives, where your data goes, who can overrule the system, what you own at handoff, and proof of a real build.

02 What are red flags when hiring an AI consultant? +
Guaranteed ROI numbers, transformation promised in weeks, prices only available after a discovery sequence, unverifiable scarcity, tool recommendations that always land on a partner product, and case studies with no names.

03 Should an AI consultant guarantee ROI? +
No — and a guarantee is itself a red flag. Real results depend on your execution, so a serious firm quotes ranges and publishes its assumptions.

04 What should you own at the end of an AI project? +
Everything: the systems, credentials, documentation, and prompts, with your team trained to run them. Ongoing help should be optional — ours is a monthly retainer from $1,500 with no lock-in.

Start here
